# FlowSpec

> FlowSpec is a declarative, engine-agnostic specification language for AI-driven acceptance testing. One FlowSpec document is one feature journey (a Flow), described as the distinct paths through it (Cases), the reproduction steps for each path (Steps), what must be true at the end of it (Assertions), and captured artifacts (Evidence) — never browser automation. Execution engines (AI browser agents, Playwright, Selenium, mobile agents) decide how to perform the actions.

FlowSpec is to AI acceptance testing what OpenAPI is to REST APIs: a framework-independent source of truth for expected behavior shared by developers, QA engineers, and AI agents.

Key facts:

- **One flow per file.** A document's top level *is* the flow — `spec`, `name`, `variables`, `setup`, `cases`, `cleanup` — with no wrapper and no `flows` array. Current spec version 1.0. Files live as plain `.json` in `.flowspec/`, named for the feature with a `_flow` suffix (`login_flow.json`, `request_quote_flow.json`, nestable). The flow's id is its filename, so it cannot collide or drift.
- **Cases are the distinct paths through the feature, not sequential checkpoints.** A login flow's cases are `valid-credentials`, `inactive-account`, `invalid-credentials`. Every case runs regardless of what the others did; array order is presentation only, and engines may run them in any order or in parallel. Case ids must be unique. There is no routing, branching, or graph between cases — a path needing a different route is a different case, and a different feature is a different file.
- **Every case is expected to pass, sad paths included.** `inactive-account` asserts the refusal appears and the user stays put; it fails only if the app lets the dormant user in. Nothing is ever authored as an expected failure, and `failed` is always a verdict on the application, never on the path being tested.
- A case is one path *end to end* — its steps are the reproduction steps. Crossing several pages does not make several cases: `navigate` is an ordinary step.
- **`setup` and `cleanup` run before and after *each case*** (`setup → steps → assertions → evidence → cleanup`), not once per flow. That is what makes the paths independent: without it, a case that signs in would leave the next one authenticated. It is `beforeEach`/`afterEach`. Setup holds the page every case starts on plus any sign-in or seeding, and must hold for all of them. Preconditions shared between flows are repeated per flow; imports are out of scope for 1.0.
- The bare filename `.flowspec.json` is the project configuration — `baseUrl`, `targetAttribute`, `output` — never a flow. With no container document, it is where settings are stated once for every flow. Settings resolve invocation → flow → config → default.
- Targets are semantic component names resolved via a data attribute — never CSS selectors or XPath. The attribute defaults to `data-constell` and is configurable via `targetAttribute` in the config or the flow, so teams already using `data-testid` or `data-qa` adopt FlowSpec without migrating markup. When the configured attribute matches nothing on the page at all, engines detect the convention the page actually uses, run with it, and report the substitution as a warning.
- Variables use `{{name}}` interpolation and are scoped to their flow; undefined references fail at load time.
- Case outcomes: passed, failed (an assertion came back false), error (a step could not execute, or setup failed). There is no `skipped` — every case runs. A failing setup step makes that case `error`, not `failed`, and the remaining cases are still attempted. The flow's status is the worst of its cases.
- `description` is optional on the flow, cases, steps, and assertions and states intent, never mechanics; engines carry it into reports, where an assertion's description becomes its failure message.
- On any failure, engines must capture at least a screenshot and console log.
- Results are written to `flowspec-results/` — `report.json` (its top level the flow: `id`, `name`, `summary`, `cases`), optional JUnit `report.xml` (one `<testsuite>` per flow, one `<testcase>` per case, nothing skipped), and `evidence/<case-id>/` artifacts referenced by relative path. Multi-flow runs nest per flow id, mirroring the `.flowspec/` tree, under a run-level summary. A case's stable identity is `<flow-id>/<case-id>`. Exit codes: 0 passed, 1 failed, 2 errored or invalid.
- Because setup runs per case, a single case is runnable in isolation and reproduces exactly what it does in a full run.

## Install

The skill is a single dependency-free Markdown file. Download it directly — `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daveconstell/flowspec/main/public/SKILL.md -o ~/.claude/skills/flowspec/SKILL.md` — or clone `https://github.com/daveconstell/flowspec.git` and run `./install-skill.sh` (no argument installs globally to `~/.claude/skills/` and `~/.agents/skills/`; pass a project path for a project-local install).

## Docs

- [Full specification](/spec-final.md): the complete FlowSpec 1.0 language specification — flow file format, cases, actions, assertions, evidence, setup/cleanup, execution lifecycle, reporting.
- [Authoring skill](/SKILL.md): a condensed skill for writing and running FlowSpec flows. Installed in an agent's skills directory it responds to eight `/flowspec` commands: `help` (command list plus setup state), `init` (bootstrap `.flowspec.json` and `.flowspec/`), `run [file] [case]` (every flow, one flow, or one case; `--url X`, `--headed`), `flow:new` (propose a feature's paths, author the confirmed ones as cases), `flow:set` (update a flow's name/description/variables/setup/cleanup), `case:new` (add a path — always asks which flow first), `case:set` (update a case — always asks which flow, then which case), and `mermaid [file]` (render a flow as one setup branching to its cases). Two standing guards: never claim a run without browser tooling actually connected, and never invent a precondition, credential, or seeded record — ask for it.

Authoring is interactive when a browser MCP is connected and the app is reachable: `flow:new` and `case:new` walk the path live rather than deriving it from source. The agent runs the flow's setup, reports the current URL and which components are reachable by target name (flagging controls that lack the target attribute), and asks what the user does next; each plain-language answer becomes one FlowSpec step, executed for real. Acceptance criteria are asked once at the end of the path and become the case's assertions — FlowSpec evaluates assertions after all steps, so a mid-path expectation is offered as a shorter separate case instead. Steps are only ever recorded as an action on a semantic target: an unannotated control stops the walk to be named first, so a walked case stays engine-portable rather than becoming selector soup.
